messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
A metric space is defined as complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point within that space. The condition provided in your prompt establishes a fundamental equivalence between this property and the behavior of nested closed sets. To prove the forward direction, assume $(M, d)$ is complete and consider a sequence of nonempty closed subsets $F_n$ such that $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ and $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$. We can select an arbitrary element $x_n \in F_n$ for each $n$. Since $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$, it follows that $x_n \in F_k$ for all $k \le n$. This implies that the distance $d(x_n, x_m)$ is bounded by $\text{diam}(F_{\min(n,m)})$, which tends to zero as $n, m \to \infty$. Consequently, the sequence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $M$. Because $M$ is complete, there exists a limit point $x \in M$ such that $x_n \to x$. For any fixed $k$, since $x_n \in F_k$ for all $n \ge k$ and $F_k$ is closed, the limit $x$ must belong to $F_k$. Therefore, $x$ lies in the intersection of all $F_n$, proving the intersection is nonempty.

To prove the converse, assume that any such sequence of nested closed sets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. Let $(x_n)$ be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in $M$. Define $F_n = \overline{\{x_k : k \ge n\}}$, which is the closure of the tail of the sequence. Each $F_n$ is nonempty and closed. Furthermore, $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ because the tail starting at $n+1$ is a subset of the tail starting at $n$. Since $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that $d(x_i, x_j) < \epsilon$ for all $i, j \ge N$. This implies that $\text{diam}(F_N) \le \epsilon$. Thus, $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. By our assumption, the intersection $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty F_n$ contains some point $x$. Since $x \in F_n$ for all $n$, and $F_n$ consists of limits of subsequences from the tail, $x$ is the limit of the original sequence $(x_n)$. Hence, every Cauchy sequence converges in $M$, meaning $M$ is complete.
